correctness.rationale: Conditioning on \(I_i=1\) leaves all remaining values uniformly permuted. If \(i\notin\{j,j+1\}\), exchangeability of \(\Pi(j)\) and \(\Pi(j+1)\) gives \(\Pr(D_j=1\mid I_i=1)=1/2\), hence zero covariance. For \(i=j\) and \(i=j+1\), direct counting gives conditional probabilities \((j-1)/(n-1)\) and \((n-j-1)/(n-1)\), yielding exactly the two displayed adjacent-entry formulas. Summing them gives every column sum \(-1/[n(n-1)]\); summing along each fixed-point row cancels in the interior and leaves \(-1/(2n)\) at the two endpoints. The wrap descent contributes \(+1/(2n)\) at those endpoints and zero elsewhere, proving exact cyclic orthogonality. With the standard \(\operatorname{Var}(F)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(D)=(n+1)/12\), the correlation formula follows. The exhaustive checker through \(n=9\) was inspected only as finite corroboration.
risks: Zero covariance is not independence; the theorem is for the uniform measure on the full symmetric group.

value.rationale: The result is a natural structural refinement of a classical joint-statistics problem: it identifies the entire cross-covariance matrix, proves that the aggregate \(-1/n\) dependence is purely an open-boundary effect, and shows cyclic closure restores exact coordinatewise orthogonality. This localization is potentially useful in multivariate limit/Stein calculations because it exposes the sparse dependence structure rather than merely another aggregate moment.
risks: The proof is elementary once the right coordinates are chosen; its value rests on the structural localization and cyclic cancellation, not technical depth.

limitations: The theorem gives second-order dependence only; it does not determine higher mixed moments or independence.
